items.stem: Explain the difference between irrational numbers and rational numbers.
items.answer: A rational number can be written as a/b with integers a, b (b ≠ 0) and has a terminating or recurring decimal; an irrational number cannot, and its decimal neither terminates nor recurs.
items.markingKey: A rational number can be written as a/b with integers a, b (b ≠ 0) and has a terminating or recurring decimal; an irrational number cannot, and its decimal neither terminates nor recurs. items.markingKey: Team Kestrel: 50.0%, Team Condor: 37.0%, Team Baobab: 58.0%; best is Team Baobab; percentages share a common denominator of 100. Conversions correct (M1 A1), comparison/remaining amount found (M1 A1), conclusion communicated in context (C1).

items.stem: A family drives 459 km from Accra on holiday. Their car uses 5.3 litres of fuel per 100 km and fuel costs GH₵1.8 per litre. (a) Estimate the fuel cost using 1 s.f. values. (b) Calculate the cost to the nearest cent. (c) Explain why the estimate is useful.
items.answer: (a) ≈ GH₵50 (b) GH₵43.79 (c) checks the calculator answer is the right size
items.markingKey: (a) ≈ GH₵50 (b) GH₵43.79 (c) checks the calculator answer is the right size. Rounded values used for the estimate (M1 A1); accurate calculation (M1 A1); appropriate rounding in context and a reasoned comment (D: R1).

items.stem: Define the term "reciprocal".
items.answer: The number which multiplies by a given number to give 1; the reciprocal of a/b is b/a
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number which multiplies by a given number to give 1; the reciprocal of a/b is b/a. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rational number"?
options: The number which multiplies by a given number to give 1; the reciprocal of a/b is b/a
A number that can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0 (the set ℚ)
A counting number 1, 2, 3, … (the set ℕ; in some texts ℕ also contains 0)
An approximate answer found by rounding the numbers in a calculation, usually to 1 significant figure
items.answer: A number that can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0 (the set ℚ)
items.markingKey: B. "rational number" is a number that can be written as a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0 (the set ℚ).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A decimal in which a digit or block of digits repeats forever, such as 0.272727… = 0.2̅7̅"?
items.answer: recurring decimal
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of recurring decimal.

items.stem: A school trip needs 88 students to travel in minibuses that hold 12 each. Priya divides and rounds to the nearest whole number. Explain why this is not appropriate here.
items.answer: 88/12 = 7.33, which rounds to 7, but that leaves 4 students behind; you must round up to 8 minibuses so that everyone travels.
items.markingKey: Division correct (A1); context requires rounding up (R1).

items.stem: Isabel writes 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/7. Explain the mistake and give the correct answer.
items.markingKey: Numerators and denominators were added separately (R1); a common denominator is needed (M1); 11/12 (A1).

items.stem: Distinguish between natural numbers and integers.
items.answer: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …; integers also include 0 and the negative whole numbers.
items.markingKey: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …; integers also include 0 and the negative whole numbers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Without dividing, explain which of the fractions 1/12, 1/16, 1/15 and 1/30 give terminating decimals.
items.answer: Terminating: 1/16; the others recur.
items.markingKey: Rule: in simplest form a fraction terminates exactly when the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5 (R1); prime factorisations shown (M1); correct list (A1).

items.stem: The side of a square tile is measured as 4.9 cm (to 1 d.p.). Chloé rounds it to 5 cm before finding the area of 100 tiles. Explain why the area should be calculated from the unrounded length.
items.answer: Exact: 2401 cm²; rounded first: 2500 cm². Rounding early creates an error that multiplication makes larger.
items.markingKey: Both areas computed (A1); rounding should be done only at the end (R1).

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Dividing always makes a number smaller." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes it larger, e.g. 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12.
items.markingKey: Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes it larger, e.g. 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write these numbers in ascending order: −2, 3/4, −3/8, 5.
Express 0.747474… as a fraction in its simplest form.
By rounding each number to 1 significant figure, estimate the value of (75.9 × 2.2) ÷ 3.1. State whether your estimate is likely to be higher or lower than the exact answer.
items.answer: ≈ (80 × 2) ÷ 3 = 53.3; exact 53.86, so the estimate is lower
items.markingKey: Each number rounded to 1 s.f. (M1); estimate 53.3 (A1); comparison with reason (R1).

items.stem: Without a calculator, evaluate (18) ÷ (−3) − (−11)².
items.markingKey: Apply the order of operations (brackets, exponents, × ÷, + −) with the sign rules (M1 M1); −127 (A1).

items.stem: "Fractions are not integers, so 12/4 is not an integer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 12/4 simplifies to 3, which is an integer; a number is classified by its value, not by how it is written.
items.markingKey: 12/4 simplifies to 3, which is an integer; a number is classified by its value, not by how it is written. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write 87.5% as a fraction in its simplest form and as a decimal.
Round 28.846 to 1 significant figure.
items.markingKey: Count from the first non-zero digit (M1); keep place value with zeros where needed: 30 (A1).

items.stem: A recipe for 4 people uses 5/4 kg of flour. Kwame wants to cook for 3 people. (a) How much flour is needed? (b) Flour is sold in 1/4 kg bags – how many bags must be bought?
items.answer: (a) 15/16 kg (b) 4 bags
items.markingKey: (a) 15/16 kg (b) 4 bags. Correct directed-number or fraction operations (M1 M1), each part answered (A1 A1), interpreted in context with units (D: R1).

items.stem: The integers between −6 and 5 are written on cards. (a) How many cards are there? (b) How many of them are natural numbers? (c) A rational card −1/5 is added – explain which set it belongs to and why it does not fit in the first group.
items.answer: (a) 10 (b) 4 (c) −1/5 is in ℚ but not ℤ, since it is a negative fraction between −1 and 0
items.markingKey: (a) 10 (b) 4 (c) −1/5 is in ℚ but not ℤ, since it is a negative fraction between −1 and 0. Method/pattern described (B: M1 A1), general rule or reason stated (R1), clear communication with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: In a school football league in Vienna, Team Lotus won 4/7 of matches, Team Kestrel won 67% of matches and Team Condor had a win rate of 0.65. Convert all three to percentages (to 1 d.p. where needed), rank the teams and explain which form is easiest for comparing.
items.answer: Team Lotus: 57.1%, Team Kestrel: 67.0%, Team Condor: 65.0%; best is Team Kestrel; percentages share a common denominator of 100
items.markingKey: Team Lotus: 57.1%, Team Kestrel: 67.0%, Team Condor: 65.0%; best is Team Kestrel; percentages share a common denominator of 100. Conversions correct (M1 A1), comparison/remaining amount found (M1 A1), conclusion communicated in context (C1).
